title: Part 1
text: Imagine a creature with no mouth, no stomach, and a diet of solid bone. It exists, and it lives on the skeletons of dead whales.

title: Part 2
text: Living among these bacteria is one of the most bizarre animals ever discovered: Osedax, nicknamed the zombie worm, or the bone-eating worm.
nxt: Researchers first found it in 2002, on a gray whale skeleton in Monterey Canyon, off California. These worms have no mouth and no stomach.

nxt: Instead, they have bright red, feathery plumes that take in oxygen from the cold seawater. Anchored to the skeleton, they look like crimson flowers blooming across a graveyard of bones.

title: Part 3
text: How can a creature without a mouth feed on solid bone? The secret is its roots. The lower part of the female Osedax grows into the bone and releases acid that dissolves it.
nxt: Inside those root-like tissues live symbiotic bacteria that break down the collagen and fats in the bone, and the worm absorbs the nutrients.

title: Part 4
text: The reproductive life of Osedax is even stranger. Every visible, feathery worm is female. So where are the males?
nxt: They are microscopic dwarves, far smaller than their mates, living inside the female's gelatinous tube, sometimes dozens in a single tube. They do not feed on bone.

title: Part 5
text: Since that first discovery, researchers have found many different species of Osedax, living on whale bones in oceans around the world.
nxt: Their larvae seem to find bones from far away, though how they do it is still being studied.

title: Part 6
text: Alongside the zombie worms, clusters of mussels, clams, and limpets settle on the bones. These animals do not filter plankton like their shallow-water cousins.
nxt: Instead, their gills host bacteria that use the hydrogen sulfide seeping from the bones. In this pitch-black graveyard, life runs on chemistry.
